title: Food Delivery App System Design (Zomato/Swiggy)
summary: An end-to-end system design of a Zomato/Swiggy-style food delivery app. It covers requirements and scale, architecture, search, menu, cart, orders, payments, rider assignment, tracking and notifications. It closes with scaling, failure handling, trade-offs and interview questions.

chapters.title: System Design of a Food Delivery App
points: Running example: a Zomato/Swiggy-style app (Food Delivery App) with about 20M monthly users
Chapter list: scope, requirements and scale, architecture
Chapter list: discovery and search, menu, cart and checkout
Chapter list: order state machine, payments, rider assignment
Chapter list: real-time tracking, notifications
Chapter list: scaling and failure handling, cheatsheet
Every subsystem chapter follows one template: responsibilities, design, flow, data model, APIs, failures, metrics
Headline scale target: 2M orders/day, 10x dinner-peak concentration, 5 s p99 order placement

chapters.title: Problem Statement and Scope
points: Three-sided marketplace: customers, restaurants and delivery partners, each with a different app and SLA
Core loop: browse, order, pay, restaurant prepares, rider picks up, rider delivers, rating
In scope: discovery, cart, orders, payments, assignment, tracking, notifications
Out of scope: restaurant onboarding and KYC, rider payouts, ads, Instamart-style grocery
Aggregator model: the app lists restaurants but does not cook, and takes a 20-30% commission
Hyperlocal constraint: supply is bound to a 5-8 km radius, so the system is partitioned by city
Time sensitivity: food is perishable, so a 40-minute SLA beats raw throughput
Peaky traffic: lunch 12-2 pm and dinner 7-10 pm carry about 60% of daily orders
Comparison with e-commerce: no warehouse inventory, menus change by the hour, delivery is a live logistics problem
Comparison with cab hailing: the extra hop is restaurant prep time, so the order has three parties instead of two
Actors and their primary actions, listed as a table
Clarifying questions to ask first: cities, vegetarian-only mode, scheduled orders, cash on delivery

chapters.title: Requirements and Scale Estimates
points: Functional: search restaurants and dishes by location, cuisine and name
Functional: view menu, build cart, apply coupon, place order, pay
Functional: track order live, get status notifications, cancel, rate
Functional: restaurant accepts or rejects orders and marks them ready
Non-functional: availability 99.95% for browse and 99.99% for the order and payment path
Non-functional: search p99 under 300 ms, order placement p99 under 2 s, tracking update lag under 5 s
Consistency: strong for orders and payments, eventual for menu, search and ratings
Users: 20M MAU, 5M DAU, 2M orders/day, which is 23 orders/s average
Peak orders: 10x average at dinner, so about 250 orders/s
Read-heavy ratio: about 100 browse/search requests per order, so about 25K search QPS at peak
Tracking load: 300K active riders pinging every 4 s gives 75K location writes/s
Storage: an order record of about 2 KB gives 4 GB/day and about 1.5 TB/year; location history is 75K x 40 B x 86,400 s, or about 260 GB/day

chapters.title: High-Level Architecture
points: Clients: customer app, restaurant tablet app, rider app and an ops dashboard
Edge: CDN for images and menus, API gateway for auth, rate limiting and routing
Core services: Search, Catalog, Cart, Order, Payment, Dispatch, Tracking, Notification
Sync calls use gRPC between services and REST at the edge
Async events go over Kafka: OrderPlaced, PaymentCaptured, OrderAccepted, RiderAssigned, Delivered
Data stores: Postgres or MySQL for orders, Redis for carts and sessions, Elasticsearch for search
Data stores: Cassandra or DynamoDB for location history, S3 for images, a warehouse for analytics
Database per service: each service owns its data and no other service reads its tables
The order path stays synchronous up to payment, and everything after it is event-driven
Shard by city, since city is the natural boundary for supply, demand and failures
Monolith versus microservices: start modular and split along order, payment and dispatch
Request walk-through: browse, cart, checkout, payment, order event, dispatch, tracking, delivery

chapters.title: Restaurant Discovery and Search
points: Responsibilities: list nearby open restaurants, search by dish or cuisine, filter, rank
Geo-index: geohash or S2 cells at about 5 km precision, with neighbour-cell lookup at the borders
Elasticsearch index per city, with documents holding restaurant, tags, rating, open status and delivery zone
Serviceability check: the restaurant must be open, the user inside its delivery polygon, and the ETA under the limit
Ranking signals: distance, rating, ETA, popularity, conversion rate and personalization
Autocomplete with a prefix index and fuzzy matching so 'pizzaa' still finds pizza
Index freshness: Kafka CDC from the catalog DB updates the index in under 5 s; open or closed status lives in Redis
Query flow: gateway, search service, geo-filter, text match, rank, hydrate from cache, return 20 results
Data model: Restaurant(id, geo, cuisines[], rating, open_hours, zone_polygon, is_open)
API: GET /v1/search?lat=&lng=&q=&filters=&cursor= returns cards with a cursor, not offset pagination
Failures: stale index shows a closed restaurant, so re-check availability at cart time; if ES is down, fall back to a Redis top-N by geohash
Metrics: search p99 300 ms, zero-result rate under 3%, search-to-order conversion, index lag in seconds

chapters.title: Menu and Catalog Service
points: Responsibilities: store restaurants, menus, items, prices, variants and availability
Menu hierarchy: Restaurant, Category, Item, VariantGroup, Addon
Read to write ratio of about 1000:1, so serve from cache and CDN with a 60 s TTL
Write path: restaurant tablet or partner portal, then catalog DB, then CDC to Kafka, then search index and cache invalidation
Item availability (stock-out) is a fast toggle that bypasses the full menu publish
Price snapshots: the order stores a copy of the item name and price at order time
Data model: Item(id, restaurant_id, name, price_paise, veg, variants_json, available, version)
Money is stored as integer paise, never as floats
Menu versioning: the cart records the menu_version, and a mismatch at checkout forces a refresh
API: GET /restaurants/{id}/menu is ETag-cacheable; PATCH /items/{id}/availability
Failure: an item sold out after it was added to the cart, so re-validate at checkout and show a substitution prompt
Metrics: cache hit rate above 95%, menu fetch p99 100 ms, menu staleness, item-unavailable rate at checkout

chapters.title: Cart and Checkout
points: Responsibilities: hold the user's selected items, apply offers, compute fees, validate, and hand off to the Order service
Single-restaurant cart rule: adding an item from another restaurant prompts the user to clear the cart
Storage: Redis hash keyed by user_id with a 24 h TTL; the cart is ephemeral and need not be durable
Price breakdown: item total + packaging + delivery fee + surge + taxes (5% GST) + platform fee - discount
Coupon engine: rule checks for min order value, first-order-only, per-user limit and validity window
Checkout steps: revalidate the cart, recheck the restaurant is open, pick the address, compute the final price, create the order
Idempotency key per checkout, so a double tap on Place Order creates one order
Data model: Cart(user_id, restaurant_id, items[{item_id, qty, addons}], coupon, menu_version)
API: PUT /cart/items, POST /cart/apply-coupon, POST /checkout returns a price quote valid for 5 minutes
Dynamic delivery fee depends on distance, demand and weather; the quoted fee is locked into the order
Failure: price changed between cart and pay, so show a diff and require re-confirmation rather than silently charging more
Metrics: cart-to-order conversion about 30%, checkout p99 under 800 ms, coupon failure rate, cart abandonment rate

chapters.title: Order Service and State Machine
points: Responsibilities: be the single source of truth for an order's lifecycle and coordinate the other services
States: CREATED, PAYMENT_PENDING, PLACED, ACCEPTED, PREPARING, READY, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED
Terminal and side states: CANCELLED, REJECTED, FAILED, REFUNDED
Transitions are validated: DELIVERED cannot go back to PREPARING, and a transition table enforces this
Optimistic locking: UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND version=? stops two actors changing the state at once
Orchestration: the Order service drives the saga, with compensating steps for refund and rider release
Outbox pattern: the DB write and the Kafka event commit in one transaction, so events are never lost
Restaurant must accept within 3 minutes or the order is auto-rejected and refunded
Data model: Order(id, user_id, restaurant_id, status, version, total_paise, address_snapshot, created_at)
Data model: OrderItem(order_id, item_id, qty, price_snapshot) and OrderEvent(order_id, from, to, actor, ts) as an audit log
API: POST /orders (Idempotency-Key header), GET /orders/{id}, POST /orders/{id}/cancel
Failures: a stuck PAYMENT_PENDING order is swept by a timeout job at 15 minutes; metrics: order success rate above 98%, acceptance time p50 40 s, cancellation rate

chapters.title: Payments
points: Responsibilities: charge, refund, reconcile and keep payment state correct across providers
Methods: UPI, cards, wallets, net banking and cash on delivery
Never store raw card numbers: use a PCI-compliant gateway and tokenization
Payment states: INITIATED, PENDING, SUCCESS, FAILED, REFUND_INITIATED, REFUNDED
Flow: create a payment intent, redirect to the PSP, user authenticates, PSP webhook confirms, the Order service is notified
Webhook handling: verify the signature, deduplicate by event id, and process idempotently
Never trust the client redirect: only a server-side webhook or a status poll confirms success
Retry and failover: if gateway A has a success rate below 90%, route new payments to gateway B
Data model: Payment(id, order_id, amount_paise, method, psp, psp_txn_id, status) and Refund(id, payment_id, amount, status)
API: POST /payments (idempotency key), POST /payments/{id}/refund, POST /webhooks/psp
Failures: the user is debited but the webhook is lost, so a reconciler polls pending payments every 2 minutes; money is moved by the PSP, and we keep a double-entry ledger
Metrics: payment success rate above 95%, p99 PSP latency, pending-payment age, daily reconciliation mismatches (target 0)

chapters.title: Delivery Partner Assignment
points: Responsibilities: find a rider for each order, minimize wait and delivery time, balance load
Trigger: dispatch starts at restaurant acceptance, timed so the rider arrives when the food is ready
Candidate search: online and idle riders within 3 km via geohash, from a Redis GEO set
Scoring: pickup distance, rider rating, current load, direction of travel and expected prep time
Matching options: greedy nearest rider (simple), batched global matching every 10 s using the Hungarian algorithm (better)
Batching: bundle 2 orders from the same restaurant or going the same direction onto one rider
Offer flow: offer to rider 1 with a 20 s timer, then rider 2, up to 3 attempts before widening the radius
Rider state: OFFLINE, IDLE, OFFERED, TO_RESTAURANT, TO_CUSTOMER
Data model: Rider(id, status, geo, rating, capacity) and Assignment(order_id, rider_id, status, attempts)
API: POST /dispatch/assign, POST /rider/offers/{id}/accept, PUT /rider/status

Failures: two dispatchers offering one rider, prevented by an atomic Redis lock; a rider dropping off mid-order triggers re-assignment; metrics: assignment time p50 30 s, offer acceptance above 70%, rider idle time

chapters.title: Real-Time Tracking
points: Responsibilities: ingest rider locations and show live position and ETA to the customer
Rider app pings GPS every 4 s while on a trip, with batching and a lower rate when idle
Ingest path: rider app, gateway, Kafka location topic, consumers
Hot store: Redis GEO holds only the latest position per rider; cold store: Cassandra with a 30-day TTL for history
Push to customers: WebSocket or SSE fan-out, with polling every 5 s as a fallback
Fan-out is cheap: each rider has one watcher (the customer), so no celebrity-fanout problem
ETA = rider-to-restaurant + remaining prep + restaurant-to-customer, using a routing engine such as OSRM and live traffic
Smoothing: snap GPS to roads (map matching) and drop jumps over 100 km/h
Data model: LocationPing(rider_id, lat, lng, ts, speed, battery) partitioned by rider_id and day
API: POST /rider/location (batched), GET /orders/{id}/track, WS /track/{order_id}
Failures: a rider goes offline in a tunnel, so show the last known position with a 'reconnecting' state and extrapolate the ETA
Metrics: location-to-screen lag under 5 s, WebSocket connection count (about 1M), ETA error under 3 minutes at p90

chapters.title: Notifications
points: Responsibilities: tell the customer, restaurant and rider about events across push, SMS and in-app channels
Triggers: every Order state change and rider event arrives on Kafka
Channels: push (FCM/APNs) is cheapest, SMS (about Rs 0.15 each) is the fallback, and in-app inbox is stored
Priority tiers: transactional (order confirmed) sent immediately; promotional batched, rate-limited and sent in quiet-hour-aware windows
Template service with localization and per-event variables
Preferences and opt-outs are checked before every promotional send
Dedup key (order_id + event) so a retried consumer never double-notifies
Retry with exponential backoff, a dead-letter queue, and channel fallback from push to SMS
Restaurant alerts need a louder path: a repeating ring and a phone-call fallback after 60 s without acceptance
Data model: Notification(id, user_id, type, channel, payload, status, sent_at) and DeviceToken(user_id, token, platform)
API: internal POST /notify (event, user, template); user PUT /preferences; stale token cleanup on provider feedback
Failures: FCM outage (fall back to SMS for critical events), token expiry; metrics: delivery rate above 97%, event-to-notification p99 under 3 s, opt-out rate

chapters.title: Scaling and Failure Handling
points: Peak handling: autoscale stateless services on QPS, and pre-scale before the 7 pm dinner peak and event days like IPL finals
Database scaling: read replicas for orders, then shard by city_id or user_id, and archive orders older than 1 year
Cache strategy: cache-aside for menus and restaurants, with TTL jitter to avoid a thundering herd
Load shedding under overload: drop promos and recommendations first, protect the order path
Circuit breakers and timeouts (for example 1 s on search) so a slow service cannot cascade
Graceful degradation: if the rating service is down, show restaurants without ratings
Multi-AZ deployment within a region; city-level failover and disaster recovery with an RPO of about 1 minute
Idempotency everywhere: orders, payments and webhooks must be safe to retry
Kafka consumer lag alerts, with partitions keyed by order_id to keep per-order ordering
Trade-off: consistency versus availability, choosing CP for payments and orders and AP for browse
Trade-off: push or pull for tracking, and greedy or batched dispatch
Common interview questions: design surge pricing, add scheduled orders, handle a restaurant going offline mid-order, prevent coupon abuse

chapters.title: Food Delivery System Design Cheatsheet
points: Scale: 2M orders/day, about 250 orders/s at peak, 25K search QPS, 75K location writes/s
Order states: CREATED, PAYMENT_PENDING, PLACED, ACCEPTED, PREPARING, READY, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED
Search: geohash plus Elasticsearch, with open status in Redis; cursor pagination
Cart: Redis with a 24 h TTL, a single-restaurant rule, and a price quote valid for 5 minutes
Orders: optimistic locking on a version column, outbox pattern, saga with compensation
Payments: idempotency key, webhook as the source of truth, reconciler every 2 minutes
Dispatch: Redis GEO within 3 km, batched matching, 20 s offer timer, 3 attempts
Tracking: ping every 4 s, WebSocket push, Redis hot store and Cassandra cold store
Notifications: push first, SMS fallback, dedup key per event, priority tiers
Latency targets: search 300 ms, checkout 800 ms, order placement 2 s, tracking lag 5 s
Mistakes to avoid: floats for money, trusting the client for payment success, shared databases, no idempotency
Interview order: scope, numbers, architecture, deep-dive the order and payment path, then failures
